questions.scenario: An insurance group is building a Claude-based tool that drafts claim-summary reports for auditors. Compliance requires documented requirements, formal validation that each output type meets specification, and sign-off before each twice-yearly release. The scope and rules are stable and fully specified up front.
questions.stem: Which systems life cycle approach best fits this project?

options.text: Short agile sprints that deploy prompt changes weekly and rely on post-release monitoring instead of formal validation
A phase-sequential (waterfall/V-model) life cycle with fixed requirements, documented design, and formal verification against the specification before each sign-off
Continuous deployment with automated canary releases and rollback, treating each prompt edit as an independently shippable change
A research phase only: prototype prompts directly with auditors in production and defer requirements and validation until usage stabilizes

questions.explanation: When requirements are stable, the deliverable is compliance-driven, and each release needs documented validation and sign-off, a phase-sequential (waterfall/V-model) life cycle fits. Iterative and DevOps-style approaches are designed for evolving products and frequent releases; here the cadence and evidence requirements are fixed by regulation, not by learning needs.

whyWrong.A: Weekly unvalidated deploys replace the formal verification and sign-off the compliance process mandates; monitoring detects problems only after auditors have already seen them.
whyWrong.C: Continuous deployment optimizes for speed the process does not permit, and canary releases produce no audit evidence of validation against specification.
whyWrong.D: Prototyping in production before requirements and validation exist inverts the phase order and ships unvalidated output into the compliance process itself.

questions.mindset: Match the life cycle model to the work: stable, regulated, validation-heavy deliverables belong in phase-gated models.

questions.scenario: A team is about to start building a Claude-powered support ticket triage feature. The product owner asks where in the life cycle the work of defining success criteria and building the evaluation set should happen.
questions.stem: What should the team lead advise?

options.text: Defer both until launch and use live production traffic as the test set, since real data is the only valid judge of quality
Wait until the model has been selected, because measurable criteria depend on which specific model the team will use
Define measurable success criteria during requirements and build the evaluation set alongside development, so it gates later prompt and model changes
Treat evaluation as an operations concern and compare each week's outputs against the previous week's to detect quality drift after release

questions.explanation: For a Claude feature, evals are the test phase for model behaviour, and they can only gate releases if they exist before the changes start landing. Measurable success criteria are defined during requirements (they express business needs, not model properties), and the eval set is built alongside development so design and build decisions are checked against a fixed standard.

whyWrong.A: Launching with no test phase means the first users are the eval; there is no baseline to gate the inevitable prompt and model changes afterwards.
whyWrong.B: Success criteria describe required business outcomes (accuracy targets, formats, limits); they are model-agnostic and should drive model selection, not follow it.
whyWrong.D: Comparing week over week uses a moving baseline with no fixed standard; drift from the intended behavior is invisible if both weeks are equally degraded.

questions.mindset: The eval set is the test phase for model behaviour — define the standard during requirements, not after launch.

questions.scenario: A customer-facing summarization feature's system prompt lives in a shared document. Engineers edit it freely, deployments copy the current text by hand, and over the past month output behavior has drifted in ways no one can attribute to a specific change.
questions.stem: What is the BEST first step to bring this feature under life cycle control?

options.text: Treat the prompt as a release artifact: move it into version control, require reviewed changes, and run the eval suite before each tagged deployment
Add an instruction to the prompt telling Claude to keep its behavior consistent regardless of any edits made to it
Rewrite the prompt from scratch with more few-shot examples for consistency and deploy the rewrite as a single large change
Restrict editing of the shared document to the ML lead but keep the same manual copy-by-hand deployment workflow in place

questions.explanation: Prompts and model IDs are versioned release artifacts for a Claude application. Without version control, tagged releases, and an eval gate, changes are untraceable and unrollbackable — exactly the drift this team is experiencing. Managing the prompt like code gives review history, attribution of behavior changes, and the ability to redeploy a known-good version.

whyWrong.B: A prompt instruction cannot compensate for an uncontrolled change process; consistency of process, not of wording, is the missing control.
whyWrong.C: A from-scratch rewrite deployed as one big unevaluated change makes attribution worse and risks a large regression, not better.
whyWrong.D: Limiting who can edit removes some chaos but still produces no version history, no eval gate, and no reliable record of what was deployed when.

questions.mindset: Prompts are release artifacts: unversioned, hand-copied prompts are untraceable and unrollbackable.

questions.scenario: A research-assistant product built on the Claude API runs long, stateful agent sessions that can last several hours. The team must ship a significant prompt and model update this month. Product requires that in-flight sessions are not disrupted, and engineering requires the ability to halt the rollout if quality degrades.
questions.stem: Which release approach BEST meets both constraints?

options.text: Apply the update server-side immediately to all traffic, including requests from in-flight sessions, and rely on fast rollback if complaints arrive
Terminate in-flight sessions at the deployment moment and restart them on the new version so that every user is on consistent behavior
Schedule the switch in an overnight maintenance window when few sessions are active, applying it to all traffic at once
Deploy behind a release flag: route new sessions to the update while existing sessions finish on the current version, expanding gradually with quality monitoring

questions.explanation: Staged, rainbow-style rollouts exist precisely to avoid disrupting long-running agents: new sessions start on the new version while in-flight sessions complete on the version they began with, and gradual expansion with monitoring preserves the ability to halt if quality degrades. Stateful sessions should not have their model or prompt swapped mid-conversation.

whyWrong.A: Changing the prompt or model under a running session shifts its behavior mid-conversation and produces inconsistent output in work users have already invested in; rollback after complaints cannot undo that.
whyWrong.B: Force-restarting sessions is the disruption product explicitly prohibited, and users lose accumulated context and results.
whyWrong.C: Sessions lasting hours can still be in flight overnight, and an all-at-once switch still gives no way to stop a bad rollout partway — it is a smaller big-bang release, not a staged one.

questions.mindset: Staged, rainbow-style rollouts let long-running sessions finish on the version they started and keep a halt lever.

questions.scenario: A support organization routes millions of tickets a month through a rules-based classifier and plans to replace it with a Claude-based one. The new classifier performs well on the team's curated test set, wrong routings are costly, and the current system's decisions and outcomes are logged.
questions.stem: Which cutover approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Switch all traffic in one change; the curated test set shows production readiness, and any misroutes can be corrected manually
Run the Claude classifier in shadow mode on live traffic, comparing its decisions against the current system's logged outcomes, then migrate traffic gradually with monitoring
Route the most complex tickets through Claude first, since they benefit most from language understanding, and expand only if those go well
Keep both classifiers running indefinitely and let support agents choose which system's routing to follow on each ticket

questions.explanation: Replacing a working production component is an implementation-phase cutover, and the lifecycle-safe pattern is validate-then-migrate. A curated test set cannot be assumed to mirror the real task distribution, so the classifier's decisions are first compared against the incumbent's logged outcomes on live traffic; migration then happens gradually with monitoring, preserving a halt-and-roll-back path. This mirrors eval guidance to test on data matching the real distribution rather than hand-picked cases.

whyWrong.A: A curated test set is not evidence of production-distribution performance; an all-at-once switch makes every live ticket part of the experiment and provides no way to stop partway.
whyWrong.C: Starting with the hardest, highest-variance tickets maximizes blast radius first; gradual exposure should begin where errors are cheapest and results are most measurable.
whyWrong.D: Per-agent choice yields inconsistent routing and no controlled comparison between the two systems; the old path is never retired and behavior differs ticket by ticket.

questions.mindset: Cut over like a lifecycle event: shadow-validate on live distribution, then migrate gradually with a halt lever.

questions.scenario: A contract-analysis feature failed in production when long documents produced truncated results (stop_reason max_tokens). The team fixed the immediate case by restructuring the prompt and raising the output limit, and the incident is now closed.
questions.stem: What should the team do in the test phase so this failure cannot silently return?

options.text: Instruct the model in the prompt to check that each summary it produces is complete before finishing its response
Raise max_tokens to the model's absolute maximum for every request in the system to leave a large safety margin
Add the failing long-document cases to the automated evaluation suite and require the suite to pass on every future prompt or model change
Keep the incident write-up on the team wiki and rely on the on-call engineer to recognize the same symptom next time

questions.explanation: In a Claude application's life cycle, evals are the regression safety net for model behaviour. Converting the incident's failing inputs into labeled cases makes the failure permanently detectable: any future prompt or model change that reintroduces truncation fails the suite before release, instead of waiting for another production incident.

whyWrong.A: Truncation is mechanical — generation stopped at the token limit — so a self-completeness instruction cannot detect or prevent it; the check itself is cut off before the model can act on it.
whyWrong.B: A blanket maximum raises cost and latency everywhere and still provides no test; the failure mode returns the moment someone tunes limits back down.
whyWrong.D: Reliance on human recall is not a control: staff rotate, memory fades, and nothing blocks the regressing change from shipping.

questions.mindset: Every production failure is future test data: turn it into a regression case that gates releases.

questions.scenario: The pinned model snapshot behind a company's document-processing service will be retired by the provider in 90 days. The service is business-critical, output quality is contractually committed, and past model releases have included behavior changes.
questions.stem: What is the BEST course of action?

options.text: Assemble an eval set from representative production traffic, run the successor model side-by-side against current outputs, and finish the verified migration before the retirement date
Keep the retired model ID in the code and add retry logic with exponential backoff so requests continue to succeed after the retirement date
Switch all traffic to the newest model release immediately to complete the migration well ahead of schedule and free the team for other work
Treat model continuity as the provider's responsibility and defer testing, since replacement models are guaranteed to preserve existing behavior

questions.explanation: Model retirement is a planned lifecycle event, not an emergency. Because model releases can include breaking behavior changes, the successor must be evaluated on representative production traffic side-by-side with the current model, and the migration completed and verified before the retirement date so the service never depends on a model that no longer exists.

whyWrong.B: Retries cannot make a retired model serve traffic; the failure is permanent, not transient, so retry logic just delays the same errors.
whyWrong.C: An immediate, unevaluated cutover gambles the contractual quality commitment on an unverified model with no comparison baseline.
whyWrong.D: Providers publish breaking behavior changes across releases; assuming guaranteed equivalence is exactly the misconception the retirement notice warns against.

questions.mindset: Model retirement is a scheduled migration: evaluate the successor, move before the deadline, verify on the way.

questions.scenario: A team wants every prompt and model change to its Claude feature gated by a regression suite of 800 labeled cases. The suite must finish overnight so results are ready for the morning stand-up, and the team also wants to keep run costs down.
questions.stem: Which mechanism BEST fits these constraints?

options.text: Fire all 800 requests in parallel through the synchronous Messages API at midnight and aggregate the results
Enable streaming on the same 800 synchronous calls so that they complete faster overnight
Reduce the suite to 20 randomly chosen cases per run to cut cost and latency
Submit the suite through the Message Batches API each night and reconcile the results by custom_id when the batch completes

questions.explanation: Nobody is waiting on each result, so this latency-tolerant bulk workload is exactly what the Batches API is for: large asynchronous jobs at reduced cost, with most batches finishing well inside the overnight window. Results are matched by custom_id rather than submission order, so the harness reconciles by that identifier. Eval and CI runs are natural batch candidates.

whyWrong.A: Parallel synchronous calls pay full price and press against rate limits — concurrency does not bypass them — while buying speed nobody asked for.
whyWrong.B: Streaming improves time to first token and perceived latency; it does not reduce cost and adds nothing to an unattended overnight run.
whyWrong.C: Shrinking coverage to 20 cases trades away exactly what the suite exists for; broad automated coverage is what makes the gate trustworthy.

questions.mindset: Latency-tolerant regression suites belong in the Batches API, matched by custom_id.

questions.scenario: A newly hired engineer joins a team that runs a Claude feature in production and asks which activities belong to the operate-and-maintain phase of the life cycle rather than to earlier phases.
questions.stem: Which activity is PRIMARILY an operate-and-maintain responsibility?

options.text: Writing the system prompt and tool schemas that the feature will use for its first release
Choosing whether each of the feature's workloads uses realtime or batch processing
Monitoring refusals, truncations, and token costs, sampling outputs for review, and feeding production failures into the evaluation suite
Defining measurable success criteria for the feature together with stakeholders and product owners

questions.explanation: Once a Claude feature is deployed, operating it means monitoring quality signals — refusals and truncation (which arrive as stop reasons on successful responses), cost and token usage, and sampled output review — and closing the loop by turning observed failures into eval cases. The other options are requirements, design, and build activities that precede operation.

whyWrong.A: Authoring prompts and schemas is build-phase work; operation consumes those artifacts under version control.
whyWrong.B: Choosing realtime versus batch is a design decision driven by who waits on each result; it is revisited at maintain time only when requirements change.
whyWrong.D: Success criteria are defined during requirements so they can shape design and become the eval standard — doing it post-deploy leaves the test phase undefined.

questions.mindset: Once shipped, the job is quality operations: signals, sampling, and feedback into evals.

questions.scenario: A prompt update degraded a live feature on a Tuesday morning, and restoring service took two days because the previous prompt existed only in email threads and a shared document with no history. Management asks what would have made rollback take minutes instead of days.
questions.stem: Which practice is the MOST direct answer?

options.text: Require two reviewers to approve prompt edits in the shared document before anyone deploys them
Manage prompts as versioned release artifacts in source control and deploy tagged versions, so redeploying the previous tag is routine
Have the model echo a prompt version number in each response so support can identify which version is live
Freeze all prompt changes after launch and only allow updates when a model retirement forces them

questions.explanation: Fast rollback is a property of the release process. When prompts are versioned in source control and deployed as tagged artifacts, the known-good version is one redeploy away; the two-day recovery happened because there was no artifact to roll back to. Reviewer counts and version labels do not substitute for a redeployable artifact.

whyWrong.A: Review improves change quality but leaves the team without a versioned, tagged artifact to redeploy — recovery would still be archaeology through email.
whyWrong.C: Even if the live version were identified, identification is not rollback; the previous text must still exist as a deployable artifact, which is exactly what was missing.
whyWrong.D: Freezing prompts avoids incidents by abandoning iteration entirely — the wrong tradeoff when a versioned process gives both safety and the ability to change.

questions.mindset: Fast rollback is a release-process property: versioned, tagged, redeployable artifacts.

questions.scenario: A two-person startup is building a Claude-powered interview-prep coach. Requirements are guesses at best, user feedback arrives weekly, and the founders want small, frequent improvements without breaking what already works.
questions.stem: Which life cycle approach fits BEST?

options.text: Fix all requirements in a single up-front specification and deliver one release at the end of a six-month waterfall
Adopt a V-model life cycle with formal verification gates between each prompt iteration before any release
Hold the feature back from users until the prompt is polished, then treat it as immutable to avoid regressions
Work in short iterations, shipping small prompt and model changes that must pass a lightweight regression eval suite first

questions.explanation: When requirements are uncertain and feedback is the primary input, an iterative life cycle fits: small, frequent releases let the team learn, while a lightweight regression eval suite acts as the safety net so improvements do not break working behavior. Start simple and add process only as it demonstrably helps — not heavyweight gates for a two-person team.

whyWrong.A: A long waterfall freezes guesses for six months and delivers learning only at the end, exactly when the founders can least afford it.
whyWrong.B: V-model formality suits stable, regulated work; here it would slow weekly learning without adding the safety that matters.
whyWrong.C: Withholding release delays all feedback, and immutability is unnecessary once a regression suite protects shipped behavior.

questions.mindset: Uncertain requirements mean iterate fast, with evals as the regression safety net.

questions.scenario: A team is about to release a combined change: a rewritten system prompt and a move to a different model tier for their Claude API feature. The feature serves paying customers, and the last big release caused a subtle quality regression that surfaced only in production.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices should the release include to make it safe? Choose TWO.

options.text: Run the versioned evaluation suite comparing old versus new behavior on representative traffic, and only enable the change if results meet the agreed criteria
Add an instruction asking the model to report any behavior changes it notices in its own outputs
Enable the change for 100% of traffic immediately and watch complaint volume for a week before deciding whether to keep it
Version the prompt and model ID together as one release artifact and log both with each request, so any regression can be traced and the previous version redeployed
Raise temperature slightly so outputs diversify and any regression effect is averaged out across users

questions.explanation: A safe release of behavior-changing artifacts combines an evaluation gate before exposure with traceability during it: run the eval suite comparing old versus new behavior on representative traffic, and ship the prompt and model ID as a single versioned artifact logged per request. The first prevents a known regression from shipping; the second makes an unexpected regression attributable and quickly reversible.

whyWrong.B: The model cannot compare itself to a previous version it never saw; self-reporting behavior changes is not a measurable release control.
whyWrong.C: Full immediate exposure turns customers into the test set and repeats the previous incident's discovery pattern; there is no gate and no halt lever.
whyWrong.E: Adding sampling randomness increases output variance and masks signals; it does not evaluate or trace anything, and degrades consistency for everyone.

questions.mindset: Safe releases = evaluate before, trace during, roll back after.

questions.scenario: The only engineer who understands a production Claude feature — its prompts, tool schemas, configuration, and deployment quirks — leaves the company in a month. The feature must keep changing after the departure, and a model retirement is already scheduled for next quarter.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices best keep the feature maintainable after the handover? Choose TWO.

options.text: Move the prompts, tool schemas, settings, and deployment configuration into version control alongside the application code, with a runbook covering deployment and rollback
Ask the departing engineer to stay on as the sole approver of any future changes, since no one else knows the quality bar
Build a regression evaluation suite from recent production inputs and outputs so future changes are gated by a documented, measurable standard
Archive the engineer's notes and Claude session transcripts in a wiki and direct future maintainers there when questions arise
Declare the feature stable, stop accepting change requests, and route all new requirements to a greenfield rewrite

questions.explanation: Maintainability is a property of artifacts and process, not of any individual. Versioned prompts, schemas, and configuration with a runbook make the system reproducible and rollback-capable by anyone, and a regression suite built from real production traffic gives future maintainers an objective quality gate — which also protects the scheduled model migration. Together they transfer knowledge as reviewable, executable artifacts instead of personal context.

whyWrong.B: Retaining one person as the single approval path preserves the exact bus-factor risk the handover is meant to remove.
whyWrong.D: Notes and transcripts are static, unversioned knowledge that decays as the system changes; they may help orientation but are no substitute for versioned artifacts and a measurable gate.
whyWrong.E: Freezing the feature only defers the problem — the scheduled model retirement forces changes regardless, and a rewrite discards working behavior without evaluation.

questions.mindset: Maintainability lives in versioned artifacts and evals, not in one person's head.

questions.scenario: Operations for a Claude-based drafting assistant currently reports only service availability and latency. The team is designing the operate-phase dashboard and wants visibility into output quality, not just infrastructure health.
questions.stem: Which TWO signals should be added? Choose TWO.

options.text: Average GPU utilization of the inference provider's servers, as reported on third-party status pages
Character length of the system prompt in each release, as a proxy for instruction complexity
The distribution of stop reasons across responses, including refusals and max_tokens truncations
Success rate of health-check pings to the API endpoint, sampled every minute
Regular review of randomly sampled real outputs scored against defined quality criteria

questions.explanation: Quality visibility for an LLM feature needs signals about the content of successful responses. Stop-reason distribution catches mechanical quality failures (refusals and truncation arrive on HTTP 200 responses, invisible to error dashboards), and scheduled scoring of sampled outputs against defined criteria quantifies subjective quality that no automated signal captures. Together they cover the failure modes users actually experience.

whyWrong.A: Provider-side GPU utilization is not observable or actionable by the customer and correlates with nothing the team can fix; it is infrastructure theater.
whyWrong.B: Prompt length is a static property of each release, not an operating signal; longer or shorter prompts do not track output quality.
whyWrong.D: Health-check success is availability — the dimension the dashboard already covers — and says nothing about what successful responses contain.

questions.mindset: Quality monitoring = stop-reason health checks plus scored sampling of real outputs.

questions.scenario: Six months after launch, a Claude feature's accuracy has slowly declined. Prompts were tweaked many times by different people, no single change looked harmful, and production failures were fixed case by case without changing how the team worked.
questions.stem: Which TWO practice changes best break this cycle long term? Choose TWO.

options.text: Regenerate the system prompt from scratch each quarter so that it never accumulates cruft
Turn each verified production failure into a labeled case in the regression evaluation suite
Increase max_tokens monthly as inputs grow so that truncation never masks other issues
Keep prompts, schemas, and the eval suite in version control and block merges that fail the suite in CI
Rotate across different model tiers weekly to avoid the system overfitting to any one model

questions.explanation: Slow decline from many small unaudited changes is a missing-feedback-loop problem. Closing the loop requires that production failures become permanent regression cases (so each fix is protected) and that changes to prompts and schemas are versioned and gated by the suite in CI (so the accumulation of unchecked tweaks stops). Together these convert quality from a memory-dependent practice into a maintained artifact.

whyWrong.A: Quarterly rewrites discard accumulated working behavior without evaluation and restart the same unaudited-change problem from a new baseline.
whyWrong.C: Ratcheting max_tokens monthly is a blunt cost increase that treats a symptom; it neither tests nor explains anything, and hides real truncation bugs.
whyWrong.E: Weekly model rotation injects behavior changes without evaluation — the same unchecked-drift pattern, now scheduled; there is no 'overfitting to one model' to prevent on the app side.

questions.mindset: Sustained quality comes from a closed loop: failures become test cases, and tests gate every change.
